name: Medang Kingdom
info: A Javanese Hindu-Buddhist kingdom, the Mataram kingdom of its inscriptions, founded by Sanjaya in 732, builder of Borobudur and Prambanan, which moved to East Java in 929 and fell to the vassal Wurawari in 1016–1017.

facts.capital: Mataram (near Yogyakarta or Muntilan); Mamrati and Poh Pitu in the Kedu Plain; Tamwlang and Watugaluh near Jombang from 929; Wwatan near Madiun
facts.founder: Rakai Mataram Sang Ratu Sanjaya, who erected a lingga at Canggal in 732
facts.predecessor: The kingdom of King Sanna, Sanjaya's uncle; before it Kalingga on the north coast of Central Java
facts.successor: The kingdom of Kahuripan, re-established by Airlangga in 1019

t: The 150 years from Panangkaran to Balitung (760–910) were the apogee of classical Javanese civilisation, when Kalasan, Sewu, Borobudur and Prambanan rose on the Kedu and Kewu plains.

Under the Shailendras Javanese fleets raided Tonkin in 767 and Champa in 774 and 787, Dharanindra took Ligor and became Maharaja of Srivijaya, and the young Jayavarman II lived at the Javanese court before proclaiming Cambodia's independence in 802.

The centre moved to East Java about 929 under Mpu Sindok; Dharmawangsa's naval invasion of Srivijaya in 990 failed, and in 1016–1017 the vassal king of Wurawari destroyed the palace and killed him at his daughter's wedding.
dyk: A 10th-century Arab account describes 1,000 boats of the Waqwaq, probably Javanese or Srivijayan, attacking Qanbaloh on the East African coast in 945–946 for ivory, ambergris and Bantu slaves; Javanese inscriptions of 931 and 1053 record labour brought from Jenggi, Zanzibar.
ev: Sanjaya erects a lingga on the hill at Canggal; the inscription names him Rakai Mataram Sang Ratu Sanjaya, lord of Mataram.
Panangkaran builds the Kalasan temple to the goddess Tara and a monastery for Buddhist monks of the Shailendra realm.
Javanese fleets raid Champa a second time and burn the temple at Phan Rang, after demolishing Po Nagar at Nha Trang in 774.
Samaratungga completes Borobudur, the stone mandala begun under Dharanindra.
The Shivagrha inscription records Rakai Pikatan's victory over a rebel in a hill fortress and the consecration of the Shiva temple at Prambanan.
On 10 May Balitung takes the throne, reunites the kingdom after thirteen years of turmoil and for the first time brings parts of East Java under Mataram.
Mpu Sindok moves the capital to Tamwlang in East Java and founds the Isyana dynasty.
Haji Wurawari attacks from Lwaram, destroys the palace and kills Dharmawangsa and most of the royal family: the pralaya of Mataram.

sections.foundation:
The Medang Kingdom, which its own inscriptions call Mataram and which this profile names as the register does, is first recorded in the Canggal inscription of 732, found at the Gunung Wukir temple southwest of Magelang. Written in Sanskrit in the Pallava script, it tells of a lingga raised on a hill in the Kunjarakunja area of Yawadwipa, a noble island rich in rice and gold, on the orders of Rakai Mataram Sang Ratu Sanjaya. Java had been ruled by King Sanna, whose long reign was wise and virtuous; after his death the kingdom fell into disunity until Sanjaya, son of Sanna's sister Sannaha, took the throne, conquered the surrounding lands and brought peace. Sanjaya seems to have come to power about 717.

The Carita Parahyangan, a Sundanese text of the late 16th century, makes Sanjaya Sanna's son, tells how Sanna was defeated by Purbasora of Galuh and how Sanjaya avenged him and ruled West, Central and East Java and Bali; romanticised as it is, its agreement with the Canggal inscription suggests a historical core. Mataram is Sanskrit for motherland; the name is first found in the Wuatan Tija inscription of 880, while Medang, perhaps from the medang hardwood tree, names the palace within it. Sanjaya was a Shaivite; his successor Panangkaran was a Mahayana Buddhist, a shift that divides historians between two rival dynasties, Sanjaya and Shailendra, and a single Shailendra house that changed its patronage.
sections.socioeconomy:
Mataram relied above all on agriculture, especially intensive wet-rice cultivation on the fertile volcanic soil of Central Java, which let the population grow and supplied the labour for the kingdom's public works. Most inscriptions record the grant of sima, taxed wet-rice land recognised by royal edict, often with part or all of its rice tax assigned to build and maintain a temple; a sima was made by opening forest or converting dry ladang to irrigated sawah, and the villages throughout the realm paid their taxes in rice. The Wonoboyo hoard of gold found in 1990, dated to Balitung's reign, with gold coins shaped like corn seeds and stamped "ta" for tahil, shows an economy partly monetised.

The reliefs of Borobudur and Prambanan show soldiers, officials, court servants, travelling musicians and dancers, food and drink sellers, couriers, sailors, merchants, even thugs and robbers, beside the farmers who were the majority. Society recognised the Hindu four varnas but applied them less rigidly than India; Pigeaud divides it into rulers, religious authority, commoners and slaves, de Casparis into the court people, the priests and monks, and the commoners. In the East Javanese period the Waharu IV (931) and Garaman (1053) inscriptions record labour imported from Jenggi (Zanzibar), Pujut and Bondan to carry and pack crops for the ports; Naerssen thinks they came by purchase or as prisoners of war made slaves.
sections.military:
The Shailendra kings were sea raiders as well as temple builders. In 767 Javanese and Kunlun ships raided Tonkin. In 774 Javanese or Kunlun vessels attacked Po Nagar at Nha Trang in Champa, carried off the temple's linga and set fire to it; the Cham inscription there describes "men born in other lands, living on other foods, frightful to look at, unnaturally dark and lean, cruel as death, passing over the sea in ships". In 787 the armies of Java, "having come in vessels", burned the temple at Phan Rang. Dharanindra (r. 780–800), hailed in the Kelurak inscription of 782 as "the slayer of courageous enemies", took the Shailendras' power to Ligor on the Malay Peninsula and rose to be Maharaja of Srivijaya, by conquest or by kinship.

Sulaiman recorded in 851 a Javanese surprise attack on the Khmer, approaching the capital by river after a sea crossing, after which the young Khmer king was punished and his kingdom made a vassal. At home the Shivagrha inscription of 856 records a war against Rakai Pikatan fought at a fortress on a hill protected by stone walls, won by his youngest son Dyah Lokapala. The Anjukladang inscription of 937 rewards a village for repelling invaders from Malayu, that is Srivijaya, and in 990 Dharmawangsa launched a naval invasion to capture Palembang: Java's envoys of 992 told the Chinese court of continuous war, and Srivijaya had recovered by 1003.
sections.governance:
The king was the chakravartin, paramount ruler, governing the nagara or kadatwan from his puri, a walled palace of wooden pavilions. Administration had two levels, the court and the wanua villages. Between them stood officials titled Rakai or Samget, landed gentry who ruled a watak of several villages and passed the king's orders to the Rama, the village heads. Balitung, king from 10 May 898, centralised authority, restricted the aristocrats' autonomy, on 12 November 904 freed all Buddhist monasteries from tax, and in the Mantyasih (907) and Wanua Tengah III (908) inscriptions listed his predecessors back to Sanjaya, perhaps to legitimise an irregular accession.

Kingship changed hands uneasily. After Lokapala's death in 885 three kings followed in two years, and from 887 to 894 there was no single ruler until Jebang and then Balitung reunited the realm; Daksha, Balitung's prime minister, issued charters on his own authority before succeeding him around 910. Queens could rule: Pramodhawardhani stood beside Pikatan, and Isyana Tunggawijaya succeeded her father Sindok. Religion and state were intertwined. Sanjaya was Shaivite, Panangkaran through Samaratungga Buddhist, Pikatan Shaivite again, yet Buddhist Plaosan, Banyunibo and Sajiwan rose in his reign, and brahmins and the sangha conducted the rituals of state. Dharmawangsa ordered the Mahabharata translated into Old Javanese in 996.
sections.impact:
The Mataram era is hailed as the classical period of Javanese civilisation. Between Panangkaran and Balitung the Kedu and Kewu plains filled with temples: Kalasan and Sari (778), the 249-structure Manjusrigrha or Sewu complex (792), Mendut, Pawon and Borobudur (completed about 825), Plaosan, and the Shivagrha of Prambanan, the largest Hindu temple ever built in Indonesia, raised by Pikatan in 856 and expanded through Lokapala and Balitung. Shailendra sculpture is counted among the finest Buddhist art in the world, and Borobudur's reliefs give the most complete rendering of the Karmavibhanga, Lalitavistara, Jataka, Avadana and Gandavyuha texts.

Javanese art spread with Javanese power. The Avalokiteshvaras of Bingin Jungut in Sumatra, Bidor in Perak and Chaiya in southern Thailand show Central Javanese influence long mislabelled Srivijayan, and the Bakong in Cambodia so resembles Borobudur that travellers or missions must have carried its design to the Khmer. The Khmer prince Jayavarman II spent years at the Shailendra court before returning around 790 to rule as devaraja and proclaim independence from Java in 802, founding the Angkor era. The name Mdaη appears in the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of the Philippines, dated 900. Balaputra, displaced in Java, became Maharaja of Srivijaya and in his Nalanda inscription of 860 claimed the Shailendra inheritance.
sections.decline:
Around 929 Mpu Sindok moved the centre of the kingdom from Central to East Java, to Tamwlang and then Watugaluh near Jombang, founding the Isyana dynasty though closely related to the old house. Van Bemmelen blames a great eruption of Merapi in Wawa's reign, the Pralaya Mataram; Krom proposed an epidemic, Schrieke the burden of temple-building on peasants who drifted east; Coedès and de Casparis saw a retreat from the Buddhist Shailendras or from Srivijayan invasion, and de Casparis noted that the Brantas valley gave access to the north-coast ports and the Maluku spice trade which the isolated Kedu plain lacked.

In the late 10th century the rivalry with Srivijaya turned to war. Dharmawangsa, who had moved the capital to Wwatan near Madiun and married his sister Mahendradatta to Udayana Warmadewa of Bali, invaded Srivijaya by sea in 990 to take Palembang; the Maharaja Sri Cudamani Warmadewa won Chinese support and repelled the invasion. In 1016–1017 the vassal king of Wurawari, in the Banyumas area, struck from Lwaram during the wedding of Dharmawangsa's daughter, destroyed the palace and killed the king and most of the royal family. Javanese accounts call it the pralaya, the debacle. Airlangga, son of Udayana and Mahendradatta and the dead king's nephew, escaped to the Vanagiri forest, rallied support and in 1019 re-established the kingdom, including Bali, as Kahuripan, its capital near the Brantas estuary.

summary: The Medang Kingdom, the Mataram of its inscriptions, was the Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of Central and later East Java from Sanjaya's lingga of 732 to the pralaya of 1016–1017, whose Shailendra kings built Borobudur and Prambanan, raided Champa and Cambodia and ruled Srivijaya, and whose last king Dharmawangsa died when the vassal Wurawari destroyed his palace.
references: R. Soekmono, Pengantar Sejarah Kebudayaan Indonesia 2 (Penerbit Kanisius, 1973)
F. D. K. Bosch, Srivijaya, de Sailendravamsa en de Sanjayavamsa (1952)
Jan Wisseman Christie, "States without Cities: Demographic Trends in Early Java", Indonesia 52 (1991)

pointDescs.732: Sanjaya erects a lingga at Canggal; the inscription names him Rakai Mataram Sang Ratu Sanjaya and records his conquest of the lands around his kingdom.
pointDescs.760: Panangkaran, a Mahayana Buddhist, succeeds; the 150 years to Balitung are the apogee of Javanese classical civilisation.
pointDescs.778: The Kalasan inscription records Panangkaran's temple to Tara and a monastery for Shailendra monks; Javanese fleets have raided Tonkin (767) and Champa (774).
pointDescs.787: Javanese fleets burn the temple at Phan Rang in Champa; Dharanindra, 'slayer of courageous enemies', carries Shailendra power to Ligor.
pointDescs.800: Dharanindra's reign ends with the Shailendras masters of Srivijaya and the Khmer under Javanese suzerainty; Jayavarman II proclaims Cambodia's independence in 802.
pointDescs.825: Samaratungga completes Borobudur; the Kedu and Kewu plains are filled with temples.
pointDescs.856: Rakai Pikatan defeats a rebel at a hill fortress, consecrates the Shiva temple at Prambanan and moves the court to Mamrati; Balaputra rules Srivijaya.
pointDescs.885: Lokapala dies; three kings follow in two years and the realm falls into turmoil.
pointDescs.890: No single ruler holds the kingdom (887–894); Bhadra's and Devendra's inscriptions record rival claims.
pointDescs.898: Balitung takes the throne on 10 May, reunites the kingdom, centralises authority and brings parts of East Java under Mataram.
pointDescs.910: Daksha succeeds Balitung in an obscure transition; peace and prosperity continue but temple-building declines.
pointDescs.929: Mpu Sindok moves the capital to Tamwlang in East Java and founds the Isyana dynasty.
pointDescs.937: The Anjukladang inscription rewards a village for repelling invaders from Malayu (Srivijaya); Sindok consolidates East Java through sima grants.
pointDescs.990: Dharmawangsa invades Srivijaya by sea to capture Palembang; in 996 he has the Mahabharata translated into Old Javanese.
pointDescs.1003: Srivijaya, with Chinese support, has repelled the invasion and resumes its embassies to China.
pointDescs.1016: Haji Wurawari attacks from Lwaram during a royal wedding, destroys the palace and kills Dharmawangsa and most of the royal family.

notes: The article is titled 'Mataram kingdom' and calls Medang its other name; the profile keeps the register's name Medang Kingdom and says so in the foundation section.
Sanjaya's accession is given as c. 717 (the Sanjaya era) and as 716 in the Wanua Tengah III list, with the first inscription in 732; the register's start 732 is the Canggal inscription.

The dual-dynasty (Sanjaya/Shailendra) and single-dynasty theories are both reported; the profile does not choose between them. The article dates Pikatan's victory over Balaputra to 852 in one place and treats the Shivagrha enemy as unknown in another.
Reign dates differ within the article (Lokapala 855–885 and 850–890; Balitung 898–910 and 899–911; Pikatan 838–850); the profile uses the dates of the main narrative.
The Waqwaq attack on Qanbaloh is attributed to 'probably the Malay people of Srivijaya or Javanese people of Mataram'; the dyk says so.
The bibliography has two works; Bosch's 1952 book is cited in the body without initials, and the profile gives it as the article does.
